Camera paths through keyframes

Source: R/camera-path.R
camera_path_3d.Rd

Describe a camera move as a timed sequence of views. animate_3d() renders the path and view_3d() plays it in the browser. Paths join with c(): each part starts from the camera the previous part ends on, and the first part from the plot's coord_3d() camera.

Usage

camera_path_3d(
  keys,
  at = NULL,
  ease = "linear",
  orientation = c("slerp", "squad"),
  position = c("catmull-rom", "linear")
)

orbit_3d(degrees = 360, duration = 4, elevation = NULL, ease = "linear")

fly_through_3d(
  path,
  look_at = NULL,
  at = NULL,
  ease = "linear",
  fov = NULL,
  roll = 0,
  position = c("catmull-rom", "linear")
)

dolly_zoom_3d(fov = 10, duration = 3, ease = "cubic-in-out")

Arguments

keys

A list of camera views, each a camera_3d() result or a named list with any of projection, azimuth, elevation, roll, distance, fov, zoom, target and oblique. A field a key omits keeps the value of the previous key, and the first key's omitted fields come from the camera the path starts from. A camera_3d() result always names its projection, so pass projection = "perspective" to it for a perspective path.

at

Key times in seconds, increasing, starting at 0. The default puts the keys one second apart.

ease

Easing of time between consecutive keys: a name such as "linear", "cubic-in-out" or "sine-in", a function mapping [0, 1] onto itself, or a list or character vector with one entry per segment. Named easings are "linear" and "quadratic", "cubic", "quartic", "quintic", "sine", "circular", "exponential", "back", "elastic" and "bounce", each followed by -in, -out or -in-out (Penner 2002, as in tweenr and CSS).

orientation

"slerp" (default) or "squad".

position

Interpolation of the target, the eye of a fly-through and the log-scaled tracks: "catmull-rom" (default) or "linear".

degrees

Turn about the vertical axis in degrees; positive values increase the azimuth. Default one full turn.

duration

Length of the move in seconds.

elevation

Elevation at the end of the orbit, reached gradually, or NULL (default) to keep the starting elevation.

path

Eye positions in data coordinates: a data frame or matrix with columns x, y and z (or three unnamed columns), one row per key.

look_at

The point the camera looks at, in data coordinates: one row for a fixed point, or one row per eye position. The default looks at the centre of the plot box.

fov

Field of view in degrees. For fly_through_3d() NULL keeps the starting value. For dolly_zoom_3d() the final value, or the start and end values; 0 stands for the orthographic projection, and a single value starts from the current camera's field of view (0 when it is parallel).

roll

Camera roll in degrees, one value or one per eye position.

Value

A ggplot3d_camera_path object.

Details

camera_path_3d() interpolates keyframes. The orientation, that is azimuth, elevation and roll together, is converted to a unit quaternion and interpolated on the sphere of rotations (Shoemake 1985): "slerp" turns at constant angular speed between neighbouring keys, "squad" adds Shoemake's spherical cubic so the angular velocity is continuous at the keys. Paths therefore pass through elevation = 90 without the spin that interpolating the angles separately produces there. The target moves on a centripetal Catmull-Rom spline (Yuksel, Schaefer and Keyser 2011), which passes through every key without cusps or self-intersections. Field of view, zoom and an explicit perspective distance are interpolated in log space, where equal steps are equal ratios, with a monotone cubic (Fritsch and Carlson 1980) that does not overshoot the keys.

orbit_3d() turns the camera about the vertical axis through the target. fly_through_3d() moves the eye along a spline through points in data coordinates, looking at a fixed or moving point; while the eye is inside the plot box the axes are left out, since the box outline they follow surrounds the camera. dolly_zoom_3d() changes the field of view while the camera moves along the line of sight so that the plane through the target keeps its size on the image; a field of view of 0 is the orthographic projection, so fov = 0 morphs a perspective view into a parallel one at constant image scale.

References

Shoemake, K. (1985). Animating rotation with quaternion curves. SIGGRAPH '85, 245-254. doi:10.1145/325165.325242

Yuksel, C., Schaefer, S. and Keyser, J. (2011). Parameterization and applications of Catmull-Rom curves. Computer-Aided Design 43, 747-755. doi:10.1016/j.cad.2010.08.008

Fritsch, F. N. and Carlson, R. E. (1980). Monotone piecewise cubic interpolation. SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis 17, 238-246. doi:10.1137/0717021

See also

animate_3d(), view_3d(), camera_3d()

Examples

over_the_top <- camera_path_3d(
  list(camera_3d(azimuth = 0, elevation = 30),
       camera_3d(azimuth = 0, elevation = 90),
       camera_3d(azimuth = 180, elevation = 30, roll = 180)),
  at = c(0, 1.5, 3), ease = "sine-in-out")
over_the_top
tour <- c(orbit_3d(degrees = 90, duration = 2),
          dolly_zoom_3d(fov = 0, duration = 2))
tour
p <- ggplot2::ggplot(mtcars, ggplot2::aes(wt, mpg, z = hp)) +
  geom_point_3d() + coord_3d(projection = "perspective")
if (requireNamespace("ragg", quietly = TRUE)) {
  movie <- animate_3d(p, path = tour, fps = 4, width = 240, height = 240,
                      file = tempfile(fileext = ".apng"))
  movie$camera[, c("time", "azimuth", "fov", "projection")]
}
